turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_pareto_train.csv: 300 real steels, process/composition
    columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B, Al, Cu, W, S, Heat treatment
    step 1 temperature, Heat treatment step 1 time, Heat treatment step 1 cooling rate, Heat treatment step 2
    temperature, Heat treatment step 2 time, Heat treatment step 2 cooling rate, Heat treatment step 3
    temperature, Heat treatment step 3 time, Heat treatment step 3 cooling rate, Secondary treatment step 1
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 1 time, Secondary treatment step 2 temperature, Secondary treatment step 2
    time, Secondary treatment step 3 temperature, Secondary treatment step 3 time, Secondary treatment step 4
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 4 time, Thermal exposure temperature, Thermal exposure time) and
    the two measured objectives `yield strength (MPa)` and `elongation (%)`
    (both at room temperature).
  - b3_htsteel_pareto_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE steels whose objectives were
    NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and the same process/composition
    columns.

Select 5 candidates that jointly span the best trade-off between HIGH yield
strength (MPa) and HIGH elongation (%). Neither objective is given for the
pool. Your 5 picks are scored by the dominated hypervolume they span in the
normalized (yield strength (MPa), elongation (%)) plane, so a set of
mutually non-dominated candidates covering the frontier beats 5 candidates
that are all strong on one axis only.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit list of
candidate_ids, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
# Analysis

I first reconstructed the Pareto front of the **training** data (yield strength vs. elongation), since neither objective is available for the pool. Sorting by yield strength and tracking non-dominated (YS, El) pairs revealed several distinct "regimes" corresponding to different alloy families/process routes:

| Regime (train analog) | Composition family | Process signature | (YS, El) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low YS / very high El | Cr18‑Ni8.75‑Ti0.4 austenitic | 1050°C anneal, 700°C/20h temper | ~280‑310 MPa, 55‑65% |
| Mid‑low YS / high El | Cr20.5‑Ni13.5‑Si2.5 austenitic | 1150°C anneal only | ~375 MPa, 53% |
| Mid YS / mid El | Cr11.25‑Ni19.5‑Ti2.9 maraging | 1050‑1175°C sol., single‑stage age ~700‑750°C | ~650‑750 MPa, 28‑34% |
| High YS / low‑mid El | Cr11.25‑Ni23‑Ti2.9‑Mo1.3 maraging | double‑stage age (720+640 / 845+710) | ~900‑1100 MPa, 20‑27% |
| Very high YS / low El | Cr12.5‑Ni8.5‑Mo0.75‑Ti0.95‑Cu1.75 | low‑temp single age (250‑550°C) | 1150‑1600 MPa, 8‑16% |

I then matched pool candidates by nearly-identical composition and process parameters to these anchor regimes, choosing the pool member closest to each training analog (to keep prediction uncertainty low) while ensuring the five span the full frontier and remain mutually non‑dominated:

- **c018** – matches the Cr18‑Ni8.75 austenitic/700°C‑temper family → high elongation, modest YS.
- **c051** – matches the Cr20.5‑Ni13.5‑Si2.5 family almost exactly (only HT1 temp differs by 50°C) → high El, slightly higher YS than c018.
- **c012** – matches the Cr11.25‑Ni19.5‑Ti2.9 maraging family (700 MPa/34% analog) → mid YS/mid El.
- **c074** – matches the Cr11.25‑Ni23‑Ti2.9‑Mo1.3 double‑aged maraging family (1000 MPa/25% analog) → high YS, moderate El.
- **c004** – matches the Cr12.5‑Ni8.5‑Mo‑Ti‑Cu family with a low‑temperature single age (250°C) → very high YS, lower El but still non‑trivial ductility (best trade point in this family, better than the extreme 1900 MPa/8% point).

Together these five span from (~300 MPa, ~60%) down to (~1200 MPa, ~15%), tracing the shape of the training Pareto front and maximizing the spanned hypervolume while remaining mutually non-dominated.

Final: c018, c051, c012, c074, c004
